name: Clavicle lengthening osteotomy

lead: Clavicle lengthening osteotomy is a surgical idea in which a collarbone is cut and lengthened to widen the shoulder span and give a broader-looking frame. In looksmaxxing it appears as an extreme, rarely performed hardmaxxing option and is not an established cosmetic operation.

An osteotomy is a surgical cut through bone; applied to the clavicle, the aim would be more bone length and so more shoulder breadth. Related operations in the surgical literature treat painful non-union and malunion after fractures. No studies or trials of clavicle lengthening for cosmetic widening were found, and registered clavicle trials concern fracture treatment, plates and pins.

paras: It is discussed as a rare option by people looking at skeletal changes that muscle cannot make. It would be done by a surgeon under anesthesia, which often involves nerve blocks, with recovery from bone surgery.

Clavicle surgery sits close to nerves and vessels. A published case series of operations for late fracture complications lists conditions such as thoracic outlet syndrome and brachial plexus neuroma among the problems treated. Anesthesia for clavicle surgery often involves nerve blocks that can affect breathing muscles.

angle.text: Hardmaxxing circles discuss cutting and lengthening the collarbones as an extreme way to widen the shoulder span and broaden the frame. It is raised as a rare option rather than an established cosmetic operation. The surgical literature on the clavicle concerns fractures and their complications.

lead: Clavicle lengthening osteotomy is a surgical procedure in which a collarbone is cut and lengthened, either gradually with an external device or in one step with a plate and graft, to increase its length. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a hardmaxxing route to broader shoulders: clavicle length sets the skeletal part of shoulder width, and a wide upper frame relative to the waist is something many posters treat as central to a masculine physique. [1][2]

Published clavicle lengthening has been reported for medical reasons. A 2013 case series described lengthening by distraction osteogenesis in five patients with a hypoplastic (underdeveloped) clavicle, and a 2022 series described lengthening in seven patients with brachial plexus birth injury to reduce shoulder pain. [3][1] Both are reconstructive reports, not cosmetic ones. For cosmetic widening, a small number of plastic surgeons, notably Indianapolis surgeon Barry Eppley, publish case descriptions and answers on their own practice sites. [4][5]

On forums the topic appears as before-and-after threads, questions about surgeons and cost, and an alternative idea of using filler to add visual shoulder width. [6][7][8] Shoulder width comes from the clavicles together with the scapulae and the deltoid muscles, so people who want a broader upper frame can pursue it through training, implants or filler over the shoulder, or, in the most invasive case, lengthening of the bone itself. [2][4]

paras: The clavicle is a slender, S-shaped bone about 15 cm long that connects the shoulder blade to the breastbone and acts as a strut holding the shoulder and arm away from the trunk. Males usually have longer and larger clavicles than females. [2] Because bone length sets the skeletal part of shoulder width, some looksmaxxers raise lengthening as a way to change it, whereas exercise changes the muscle around the shoulders but not the bone itself.

An osteotomy is a surgical cut through bone. In distraction osteogenesis the cut bone ends are separated slowly with a fixator so that new bone forms in the gap, a method long used to lengthen limbs. [9] The 2013 series used a monolateral external fixator on the collarbone. [3]

The clavicle is the first bone to start ossifying, in the fifth and sixth weeks of gestation, and one of the last to finish, at roughly 21 to 25 years of age. [2] The overall look of the shoulders depends on the clavicles, the position of the scapulae and the bulk of the deltoids and upper back, which is why training, implants and filler are discussed alongside the bone-lengthening option. [2][8]

Interest in broad shoulders connects to research on male body shape. A 2025 study in Personality and Individual Differences had 283 participants in Beijing, Lithuania and Aberdeen rank 15 DXA body images that varied in shoulder-to-waist ratio and body fat. The authors reported the highest ratings near a ratio of about 1.57, with no significant gain above that, and that body fat predicted ratings more consistently than shoulder-to-waist ratio. [10]

Distraction osteogenesis was proposed in the nineteenth century, Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, and Gavriil Ilizarov developed modern external fixation and separation rates from the 1950s. [9] The method has a latency period of about a week after the cut, a distraction phase in which the device separates the bone ends at roughly 1 mm per day, and a consolidation phase while new bone hardens, followed by device removal. [9]
Reported complications across distraction procedures include infection (about 5 percent overall), hardware failure and nerve injury. [9]

Clavicle surgery in the wider literature addresses fractures, painful non-union, hypertrophic malunion and related nerve and vascular problems. A 2003 series of 17 patients treated late complications from high-energy clavicle injuries, including painful non-union, thoracic outlet syndrome and brachial plexus neuroma. [11]

Anaesthesia papers describe regional nerve blocks, including interscalene and cervical plexus blocks, for clavicle operations, and note that interscalene injection can cause temporary paralysis of one half of the diaphragm. [12][13]

A 2013 retrospective review in the Journal of Pediatric Orthopedics reported five patients (seven clavicles) with clavicular hypoplasia, with diagnoses including Klippel-Feil syndrome, cleidocranial dysplasia, Noonan syndrome, congenital myopathy and obstetric brachial plexus injury. Mean age was 15 years and mean follow-up 35 months. Mean length gained was 31 mm, about 24.7 percent of overall bone length. Mean time in the fixator was 174 days. Two patients needed internal fixation after the fixator came off to consolidate union and one needed additional fixation for atrophic regeneration. Oxford shoulder score rose from a mean of 28.5 to 41, all patients were extremely satisfied, and two developed pin-site infections. [3]

A 2022 paper in the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery described a lengthening osteotomy in seven patients (median age 20) with brachial plexus birth injury, a condition in which the clavicle can be shortened and the scapula malpositioned, overloading shoulder muscles. After a median follow-up of 42 months the authors reported that patients were satisfied. [1] A 2015 letter questioned whether congenital clavicular hypoplasia is a real indication for distraction lengthening. [14]

Cosmetic versions of the operation appear mainly on surgeons' own practice pages and in forum threads rather than in published case series. Eppley describes an approach in which the clavicle is cut and a cadaveric bone graft is placed in the gap, stating that about an inch per side can be added and that once healed no loss of function is expected, comparing recovery to that of a healed clavicle fracture. [4]

A 2022 case report on his educational site describes a very muscular man whose clavicles were under 16 cm and strongly S-shaped. The patient stopped weightlifting for four months beforehand and did shoulder stretching. The surgeon made split osteotomies of both clavicles through small incisions, slid the outer segments out to a 15 mm gap, fixed them with a screw and a long S-shaped plate, and filled the defects with donor bone putty. The report gives no measured width change and only a four-day postoperative X-ray check. [5]

The same surgeon presents deltoid or shoulder implants as the main alternative, saying they can give a similar widening effect with faster recovery and less scarring, and that osteotomy makes most sense when no other option is available. [4] He also states that whether a patient's desired widening is surgically possible depends on shoulder photographs and imaging rather than measurements alone. [15] Forum users discuss the same trade-off, along with shoulder filler as a non-surgical way to add visual width. [8][6]

The reconstructive series above report pin-site infection, incomplete consolidation needing further fixation and a long period in an external device. [3] Clavicle surgery lies close to the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels, and the late-complication literature describes neurogenic and vascular thoracic outlet syndromes among the problems that clavicle injuries and malunions can cause. [11] No published complication data exist for lengthening done for cosmetic shoulder widening.

Human studies of clavicle lengthening are limited to small reconstructive series: five patients with clavicular hypoplasia in 2013 and seven patients with brachial plexus birth injury in 2022. [3][1] No studies found of the operation for cosmetic shoulder widening in people with normal clavicles, apart from the single-patient surgeon case description noted above. Registered clinical trials on the clavicle concern fracture treatment with slings, plates and pins. [16][17]

Looksmax.org has threads titled around clavicle lengthening results, cheapest surgery, surgeons who perform it, and a claim of more than 3 cm gained per side with distraction. [6][7][18] Another thread proposes shoulder filler as an alternative to clavicle lengthening, with the author calling it a theory and suggesting it might add roughly an inch of apparent bideltoid width. [8]
On T Nation, clavicle lengthening is mostly a recurring joke: users tease each other about it in training logs, and one poster says they miss threads on clavicle widening surgery. [19][20]

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck proposes the bone-lengthening principle that later becomes distraction osteogenesis. [9]
Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical limb-lengthening attempt. [9]
Gavriil Ilizarov develops external fixation devices and separation rates that make distraction widely usable. [9]
Series of 17 patients operated on for late complications of clavicle fractures is published. [11]
First reported clavicle lengthening by distraction osteogenesis for clavicular hypoplasia (five patients). [3]
A letter questions whether congenital clavicular hypoplasia is a real indication for distraction lengthening. [14]
Clavicle lengthening reported for shoulder pain in brachial plexus birth injury (seven patients). [1]
Surgeon Barry Eppley publishes a case report of cosmetic clavicle lengthening in a muscular man. [5]
Study of 283 raters reports shoulder-to-waist ratio and body fat effects on male attractiveness ratings. [10]
